title: Reproduction by fission is a physical tendency to segment plus regeneration

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Reproduction by fission is a physical tendency to segment plus regeneration

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Reproduction by fission in worm-like animals consists essentially of the physical tendency of a long semi-fluid tube to break into segments, combined with ordinary regeneration, which explains its occurrence in zoologically unrelated animals and its absence in some close relatives.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: If we add to this natural tendency towards fission of a cylindrical or tubular worm, the ordinary phenomenon of regeneration, we have all that is essentially implied in “reproduction by fission.”

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter III, “The Rate of Growth”; topic “Regeneration”. Scope: worms and worm-like animals that reproduce by fission

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch03-33: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.35

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The regeneration component is measurable, but the claimed essential physical cause needs synchronized mechanics and molecular observations. Existing comparative and imaging records are too incomplete to discriminate passive instability from active fission programs.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Quantify spontaneous break locations and stresses in living worm-like animals, then test whether physical instability of a long semifluid tube predicts fission across taxa after accounting for active cellular patterning; separately verify regeneration of missing parts. Refutation would be patterned fission preceding mechanical instability or requiring specific molecular programs absent from nonfissioning relatives.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Comparative occurrence alone cannot distinguish passive breakage from regulated development.

The proposed physical tendency lacks a unique quantitative model.

Mechanical state at the instant of fission is not represented in broad public datasets.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claim combines a physical instability with ordinary regeneration and uses taxonomic distribution as evidence. Body form and fission mode can be compiled for a subset of annelids and flatworms, which is enough for a partial test. The mechanical wavelength is rarely measured, and developmental control of the fission plane is an alternative that existing descriptions often favour without a clean force measurement.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Test whether fission in worm-like animals occurs at the wavelength predicted for breakup of a fluid cylinder of that diameter and viscosity, and whether fission tracks that geometry across unrelated groups rather than tracking clade. Agreement with the mechanical wavelength, including in close relatives of similar shape, would support the claim; fission at genetically fixed stations independent of tube dimensions would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Stereotyped fission planes in short flatworms already sit poorly with a pure fluid instability.

Regeneration after a cut is observable, but the 'tendency to segment' is not a separate measured force.

Fission position, body diameter and regeneration are not in one trait table.
